PRODUCT DESIGN CASE STUDY

Bizinc

BIZINC · TWO-SIDED MARKETPLACE · LIVE PRODUCT

One business.
Two sides of the experience.

At Bizinc I worked on both sides of the marketplace: helping people find a service, and helping business owners manage what happens after someone finds them.

MY ROLEUI/UX Intern → Product Designer → UI/UX Manager
WHENApril 2024 – May 2026 · Remote
MY CONTRIBUTIONJourney mapping, Business Profile 2.0, marketplace and booking interfaces, operator tools, component library and handoff.
PROBLEM

One platform had to help customers discover and choose businesses while giving owners the tools to manage the identity and services those customers see.

MY OWNERSHIP

Journey mapping, Business Profile 2.0, marketplace and booking interfaces, operator tools, component library, handoff and later design-team leadership.

KEY CONSTRAINT

The platform was already live with existing businesses and categories, so owner controls and customer navigation had to evolve without fragmenting the shared profile.

OUTCOME / PROOF

Live product. Existing project records report +38% retention and +45% dashboard activation during the redesign period; individual design causality was not isolated.

KEY STAGE 01 · STRUCTURE & PROFILE

02 Two audiences, one platform.

One person manages a business. Another decides whether to choose it. The profile has to serve both.

Problem

A customer needs to understand a business and take the next step. The owner needs to edit its identity, publish offers and run the work behind that public presence.

Constraint

The platform was already live. The redesign had to support existing businesses and different service categories without turning owner tools into customer navigation.

Decision

I mapped the journeys separately, then reconciled them into one site map. Business Profile 2.0 uses a personalised profile with deliberate Business View and Client View differences.

Evidence

The written requirements and profile design make those differences visible: what the owner edits, what the client sees, and where a public profile leads to an enquiry or booking.

01 / DESIGN DETAIL

A recognisable business.

Brand imagery, profile details, opening hours and verification signals establish the identity clients evaluate.

02 / DESIGN DETAIL

Control belongs to the owner.

Products, services, deals, discounts and promotions can be managed alongside profile completion and verification.

03 / DESIGN DETAIL

Visibility is deliberate.

Business View holds management tasks; Client View presents the public-facing profile. The design includes a public URL for sharing.

KEY STAGE 02 · DISCOVERY

03 Discovery that supports a decision.

A useful card helps someone form a shortlist before opening another page.

Problem

A directory can show plenty of businesses without helping someone decide which one meets their need.

Constraint

Visitors compare different categories and locations. Business identity alone is not enough: relevance, distance and opening hours can change the choice.

Decision

I brought the service description, location, proximity and open-now status into each card, alongside a direct route to the full profile.

Evidence

The interface exposes these signals at the comparison stage. Whether they shorten time to enquiry remains a question for instrumented testing.

KEY STAGE 03 · MAP & AI PROPOSAL

04 From search to booking.

The assistant’s value depends on what a visitor can actually do after the conversation.

Problem

A visitor may know the service, place and time they need without knowing which local business to search for.

Constraint

Useful recommendations depend on business relevance, location and genuine availability. A conversational interface alone cannot establish those facts.

Decision

I proposed connecting the Bizzy assistant to nearby-business discovery and the map: clarify the request, compare matching businesses, then offer a route toward a booking.

Evidence

The Figma proposal shows the conversation moving from a service request to a time, a shortlist and a confirmation. It demonstrates the intended interaction, not a verified production integration.

Need & location→Relevant businesses→Availability & booking
Relevance and ROI are decision gates.

A useful next test would compare assistant-led discovery with direct search, measuring relevant enquiries and completed bookings. ROI is undisclosed; the reported retention increase does not establish the effect of this proposal.

The map and AI-assisted flow are presented as proposed work. This case study does not claim that every interaction in the prototype shipped.

DESIGN EVIDENCE

PROPOSED / TO VALIDATE

AI-assisted discovery

The assistant-to-booking path needs validation against relevance, real availability, completed bookings and operating cost.

Reported outcomes and their limits

Retention increased by 38%, as reported by Jamiu. The existing project record also reports +45% dashboard activation, +23% customer growth and +12% service activity across the redesign period. ROI is undisclosed.

These are product-level outcomes alongside the design work. Baselines, exact measurement dates and analytics methods are not published here, and the contribution of individual changes was not isolated.

LEARNINGS & NEXT STEPS

06 A shared profile needs explicit boundaries.

What I learned

Writing the business and client requirements side by side made each difference deliberate. Separating the journeys first gave the shared screens a clearer purpose.

What I would test next

  • Do location, distance and open-now signals shorten the path to a relevant enquiry?
  • Which owner tools encourage meaningful return visits, rather than profile edits alone?
  • Does assistant-led discovery improve completed bookings enough to justify its cost?
